courses.examProfile: HARD exam — favour multi-step questions over recall. Two sections. SECTION A (Theory): closed multiple-choice. Generate many mc and some tf questions; distractors must be genuinely tricky plausible misconceptions; the expected answer must be detailed and explanatory (teach the concept, do not just name the correct option). SECTION B (Practical): hand-written ARM assembly. Generate pseudocode-type questions that ask the student to WRITE real ARM Thumb assembly (NOT generic pseudocode) — bit manipulation (shift + AND/ORR/BIC to test/set/clear a bit), comparison + conditional branching, loops, recursion, and functions following the calling convention (args in r0-r3, return in r0, BL/BX LR, stack PUSH/POP). The expected answer must contain a fenced ```arm block with a correct, hand-writable solution. Apply Section-B coding questions to assembly/coding-capable chapters (ARM ISA, data representation, workflow); for conceptual chapters (architecture, FPGA/Edge AI) lean on hard mc/tf plus detailed written questions. Skew all difficulty to hard.

courses.name: Numerical Methods
courses.visualStyle: Formula-sheet exam. Lead with the formula in code/KaTeX, then a one-line numeric example. Use HTML/SVG diagrams for method workflows (Newton step, divided-difference table, Simpson rule, Euler/RK step, power method).
courses.examProfile: HARD resit exam — closed book + supplied formula sheet + calculator, 2 hours, 6 questions (one per topic). Each question has part (a) computational (highest marks; apply a method to specific numbers) and parts (b-e) conceptual follow-up (convergence order, error bound, when does this method fail, method choice and why, derive a simple identity). GENERATE: many "calc" questions asking for one-step numerical applications (one Newton iteration, one Simpson sub-interval, one Euler step, build a divided-difference cell, one power-method iteration); "written" short-answer questions for conceptual follow-up (state convergence order; identify failure conditions; compare two methods; explain why a method suits a problem); "mc" for must-know definitions and method-recognition. AVOID "pseudocode" and "tf" — this is a quantitative math exam, not an algorithm or true/false course. For every "calc" the "expected" must include the worked numeric answer, 1-2 line method, and the relevant formula. Skew difficulty to HARD. Prioritise Topics 1 (root finding), 3 (polynomial interpolation), 4 (numerical integration/differentiation) for both quantity and depth — these are the formulaic high-yield topics for a pass-targeted resit. Topics 2 (ODEs), 5 (least squares), 6 (eigenvalues/linear algebra) still get coverage but less depth.
